item.title: Store Memory: D2C In The Age Of Experiential Retail
item.dc:creator: Meha Agarwal
item.description: Remember the charm of walking into a Crossword store, picking up a book and spending hours reading it without anyone…
item.content:encoded:
Remember the charm of walking into a Crossword store, picking up a book and spending hours reading it without anyone expecting you to buy it? With cosy reading corners, a café on the side and occasional author interactions, it gave book lovers a place to unwind, explore and lose themselves in stories. Or Hamleys, where little eyes light up and young hearts skip a beat at the sight of colourful toys and a magical world that feels straight out of a storybook.

Brands such as Pepperfry have also made shopping more personal by letting customers experience how furniture and décor would look and feel in fully furnished living rooms, bedrooms and dining spaces. Chumbak, meanwhile, brings its playful personality to life through colourful interiors and distinctive designs that make its stores as vibrant as the products on display. Of course, how can one forget Decathlon?

Long before experiential retail became a buzzword, these stores gave customers several reasons to visit beyond simply making a purchase. 

Now, a new wave of fashion and lifestyle brands is borrowing this playbook to take experiential retail a step further. Rather than simply creating attractive spaces or encouraging product discovery, brands such as Gully Labs, Comet, Nothing, Almost Gods and Broadway are experimenting with store design and riffing on traditional retail motifs to bring their brand identity to life.

Take Comet’s flagship store in Bengaluru’s Indiranagar, for instance. With shattered walls, suspended rock formations and sneakers seemingly emerging from concrete, the space resembles the aftermath of a comet crashing to the ground rather than a conventional footwear showroom.

Yet, the experience isn’t just about aesthetics. Instead of crowding shelves with inventory, Comet displays a curated selection of sneakers, with additional sizes stored in concealed drawers. Its dedicated section, The Vault, showcases sold-out sneakers like museum exhibits, even though they are no longer available for purchase. 

The D2C sneaker brand spent around seven to eight months designing and building the store, working with an architecture firm to bring its unusual concept to life.

While store design has increasingly become a way to communicate brand identity, build communities and create unique experiences, how are brands balancing creative ambition with the unit economics realities? And can their distinctive retail experiences become a lasting competitive advantage? 

Reinventing The Storefront

For years, the conventional retail store followed a familiar pattern. Products occupied shelves, promotional displays highlighted the latest collections, and layouts were designed to move shoppers towards the billing counter.

That formula works, but does not really motivate customers, who can buy almost anything from their phones, to make the effort to visit a store. The reason is simple. They are looking for more than a transaction. 

The influence of this thinking is visible at Broadway, a multi-brand fashion and lifestyle retailer housing more than 200 brands. Rather than relying entirely on merchandise displays, it has integrated services and activities that encourage customers to explore products in different ways.

For example, its stores feature salon experiences for beauty product trials and sampling, alongside dedicated stages where brands can organise events and interact with their communities. It also offers AI-assisted analysis to help shoppers identify shades and products that suit their skin tones and complexion, with stylists able to recommend products accordingly. 

However, the process involves continuous experimentation. “A service that appears attractive during planning may not necessarily appeal to customers once introduced. These decisions are refined based on customer behaviour rather than treated as permanent elements of the original design,” said a sectoral expert.

But the push towards experiential retail is not being driven by changing consumer expectations alone. For digital-first brands, it is also becoming a question of customer acquisition. 

Ujwal Sutaria, founding partner at VC firm TDV Partners believes the rising cost of digital advertising is making physical stores an increasingly interesting brand-building channel. 

“Digital acquisition costs in India have become brutal, and a store on a 100 ft road can work as a better ad than any Instagram budget,” Sutaria said.

This is particularly relevant for brands selling premium products. For a shopper considering a pair of sneakers north of ₹5K, the opportunity to examine the product, understand its craftsmanship and experience the brand firsthand could help overcome hesitation that digital advertising alone may struggle to address.

Are There Execution Challenges?

According to Mitali Juneja, creative director at architectural design planning and studio, Studio Ordonnance, the architecture firm behind Comet and Almost Gods’ stores, most established retailers still prefer conventional formats.

The hesitation may not be financial. In larger organisations, proposals have to go through multiple levels of approval. Also, many decision-makers could be wary of committing to unfamiliar or unconventional ideas. 

On the flip side, founder-led brands have greater flexibility to experiment, offering the reason why some of the more visible experiments are emerging from younger brands rather than established retail chains.

Next, even after a concept is approved, a transition to a physical space can be difficult. Unconventional installations often require techniques that local fabricators have little experience with. 

For Comet’s suspended rock structures, for instance, Mitali’s team had to repeatedly guide workers accustomed to making traditional sculptures.

To minimise errors, detailed working drawings and inspections at different construction stages are needed. Architects must also adapt designs to the property’s structural limitations, including ceiling heights and building specifications.

However, she believes the bigger challenge is balancing creativity with functionality. Product visibility, customer comfort and the ease of trying or purchasing merchandise cannot be compromised simply to create an unusual-looking store.

The goal, therefore, is not just to deliver an impressive space, but one that works equally well for the brand and its customers.

Can The Experience Pay For Itself?

For fashion and lifestyle brands already grappling with high rentals and operating costs, the question is whether a distinctive store can generate enough value to justify the additional investment.

Sutaria believes that looking at store-level sales alone misses the wider contribution of experiential retail. A customer may discover a sneaker brand offline, try its products and eventually purchase online. Similarly, a store event could generate interest well beyond its immediate neighbourhood.

“Store P&L alone is the wrong lens. I’d look at the halo effect: Is online traffic and conversion rising in nearby pincodes? What’s the blended CAC for customers who discover the brand in-store? Do they repeat more often?” Sutaria explained.

However, the challenge is establishing whether these interactions generate additional business or simply create visibility. For multi-brand retailers such as Broadway, this becomes even harder, as product trials, sampling and engagement with individual brands may not immediately translate into sales.

Yet, the investment can pay off. According to Comet cofounder Utkarsh Gupta, its Indiranagar flagship achieved a seven-month capex payback despite costing 20–50% more than a conventional store. He also claims it records the highest conversion rate among footwear stores on that high street.

However, Sutaria cautions that the economics must ultimately justify the experience. “If the store lowers blended CAC and improves repeat rates enough to lift brand-level LTV, the capex is justified. Otherwise, it’s just an expensive billboard.”

Can Every Store Be A Flagship?

Even if an experiential store delivers strong returns, replicating the same concept across dozens of locations can be expensive and time-consuming.

Comet is addressing this by standardising most of its design elements while experimenting at select locations. According to Gupta, nearly 90% of the brand’s design elements are scalable, allowing it to retain a consistent identity without repeating the seven-to-eight-month development process required for its first flagship.

However, Sutaria also believes that most single-brand D2C companies will follow a different approach. “The scalable version is a hub-and-spoke model: one or two flagships build culture, while smaller formats and shared-shelf platforms drive reach. That’s why Broadway is interesting. Its 40,000 sq ft Bandra flagship houses 200+ brands, spreading the cost of the experience across multiple businesses.”

Such shared formats could offer emerging fashion and lifestyle brands access to product discovery, sampling and community engagement without requiring each to build an expensive standalone store.

Still, expansion is not the only challenge. An elaborate store can lose its novelty, while excessive investment in physical retail can divert resources from product development and distribution.

Juneja of Studio Ordonnance believes some experimental design elements will eventually disappear because they are impractical. However, she expects the broader shift towards stores that express a brand’s identity to continue.

The real test, therefore, will be creating spaces that remain distinctive without compromising the shopping experience or the economics of running a retail business.

THE STARTUP SPOTLIGHT | HOW KOBSOOK IS BRINGING NEURODIVERGENT ARTISTS TO SNEAKER DESIGN 

  • KobSook turns original artwork by neurodivergent artists into limited-edition canvas sneakers. The brand works with AEMP (Inclusive Accessible TechEd) as a training partner to help artists develop skills in design and other business operations.
  • Its portfolio spans high-tops, low-top sneakers, loafers and slip-ons for men and women, with designs featuring doodles, abstract patterns, colourful checks and other original artwork. Products listed on its website span roughly ₹1,700 to ₹2,500 at sale prices.
  • KobSook produces limited quantities of each design rather than relying on mass production, and also accepts requests for customised designs. The brand sells through its own website and ecommerce marketplaces including Myntra, Amazon, AJIO and Flipkart.

The Deep Dive

Ecommerce Buzz

  • L Catterton Bets On Glance: The consumer-focused investment firm has invested in InMobi-backed Glance to support the latter’s US expansion. Currently, Glance uses agentic AI to drive product discovery and purchases across smartphones and connected TVs, including through partnerships with Samsung, Motorola and DIRECTV in the US.
  • Myntra Swings To Loss: Flipkart-owned Myntra reported a net loss of ₹581.8 Cr in FY26, reversing a ₹546.3 Cr profit a year earlier. This came on the back of its operating revenue falling 13.5% to ₹5,242.5 Cr.
  • Swiggy’s Pivot To Inventory Model: Swiggy will begin shifting Instamart to an inventory-led model by mid-Q3 FY27, with the transition expected to take 2–3 quarters and improve contribution margins by 80 basis points. The move comes as Instamart’s adjusted EBITDA loss widened to ₹895 Cr in Q2 FY27
  • PharmEasy Veterans Raise ₹63 Cr: Founded by five former PharmEasy executives, Chapter Homes raised ₹63 Cr at a valuation of nearly ₹1,000 Cr. The startup plans to expand beyond its HOKIPO home furnishings brand into cookware, home décor and small kitchen appliances, using AI and a shared supply chain to scale its portfolio. 

The Operator Question

How can pop-up shops at festive carnivals (Durga Puja/Diwali/Christmas melas) help unconventional new-age lifestyle brands? What is the cost involved? Is it worth the investment? How should brands measure the ROI?

Speaking to Inc42, Cure By Design founder Daanish Matheen spoke about the pop-up shop aspect of D2C retail. The startup offers hemp-based CBD oils, balms and pain-relief solutions, alongside personal care and nutrition products such as shampoos, face washes, serums and food items.

For unconventional lifestyle brands like Cure By Design, festive pop-ups offer an opportunity to reach new audiences, build trust, and increase brand awareness. Since cannabidiol (CBD) is still an emerging category in India, these events allow the brand to educate consumers, address misconceptions, and encourage first-time purchases.

Costs vary depending on the event, location, and footfall, with expenses including stall rentals, staffing, logistics, and branding.

We’ve participated in pop-ups occasionally but have reduced them significantly since opening our retail stores in Bengaluru and Chennai. Permanent stores provide better customer engagement, stronger credibility, and more consistent conversions.

For us, ROI goes beyond immediate sales. We evaluate customer acquisition costs, leads generated, repeat purchases, and long-term customer value. Ultimately, pop-ups are worthwhile when they attract the right audience and build lasting customer relationships rather than simply generating footfall.

item.title: Ather Cracks Profitability In Q2, But Can It Sustain The Momentum?
item.dc:creator: Gaurav Bagur
item.description: Q2 FY27 marked a major milestone for Ather Energy as the listed electric vehicle (EV) major turned profitable for the…
item.content:encoded:
Q2 FY27 marked a major milestone for Ather Energy as the listed electric vehicle (EV) major turned profitable for the first time. 

The Tarun Mehta-led company reported a consolidated net profit of ₹1.3 Cr during the quarter under review compared to a net loss of ₹154.1 Cr in Q2 FY26 and a net loss of ₹51.1 Cr in the preceding quarter. 

This was also the first EBITDA-positive quarter for Ather as margins improved to 4.9% from -9.6% in Q2 FY26. Excluding other income, the EV maker’s EBITDA margins stood at roughly 0.8-1%, while adjusted gross margins further improved to 24%. 

With this, the EV maker has achieved a milestone that most of its new-age rivals, including listed Ola Electric, is yet to crack. Such is the contrast that Goldman Sachs recently downgraded its outlook on Ola Electric to “sell”, citing the Bhavish Aggarwal-led company’s challenging path towards turning positive cash flow.

However, Ather is not yet “out of the woods,” insisted CEO Mehta during the company’s earnings call. Rather than prioritising profit after tax (PAT), he said that the company is focused on capacity addition to ramp up its sales volumes and bolster its top line. 

Hence, it is planning to invest ₹122 Cr to expand the combined capacity of its existing factory in Karnataka’s Hosur and its upcoming unit at Maharashtra’s AURIC by another 2.25 Lakh units per year. This would bolster its total installed capacity to 11.4 Lakh units by Q2 FY28 – a core part of its medium-term strategy. 

With its maiden profitability quarter out of the way, how is Ather planning to continue the momentum going forward?

Fixing The Capacity Gap

Ather believes that capacity addition is its crucial bottleneck as supply, and not demand, is the overhang on its performance. 

“Pre-orders are up 108%, registrations are up 60% and production is up 45%, all year on year,” noted Mehta. He added that while the company sold 33,000 units a month in the previous quarter, their internal estimates indicated unrealised sales of 20,000 units a month. 

Hence, the Hosur capacity addition could have an immediate impact. Given the factory is already up and running, Ather plans to scale the installed capacity of 35,000 units per month at the unit by another 6,000 in Q3 FY27 itself. That said, the expansion at its AURIC plant could take longer as it will only go live by Q4 FY27. 

On the margin front, Mehta explained that elevated commodity prices of raw materials like aluminium, copper, and plastics hurt gross margins by 9.4% during the quarter. He, however, added that temporary interventions like price hikes temporarily managed to counter these elevated costs. 

“We believe roughly 5.3% of the (overall) margin improvement we have driven over the last two quarters is broadly structural in nature. This is largely because price hikes seem to have landed well in the market… More temporary levers include SKU management and pulling back incentives or other support mechanisms,” added Mehta. 

However, he noted that the company will only be able to utilise the aforementioned internal ‘temporary levers’ (which brought 2.7% in margin improvement between Q4 FY26 and Q2 FY27) for a finite period if supply constraints and commodity prices remain elevated. 

“If either situation eases, we may open up these levers (incentives and more SKUs) again,” added Ather CEO. 

Why Konarc Is The Key To Ather’s Future

Ather’s recently launched mass-market model Konarc appears to be one of the critical pieces that has unlocked its profitability. The company plans to focus on this segment to foster growth going forward. 

“Konarc focuses on the fundamentals, targeting more petrol-scooter buyers to buy electric,” Mehta said. He cited features that cater to the mainstream audience’s practical needs, such as 14-inch front wheels, longer rear suspension, a metal body, a centre stand and a 10-year battery warranty. 

Konarc also offers a potential margin advantage compared to other products like Ather’s Rizta. The model is already a few thousand Rupees lower than Rizta on a like-for-like basis, and the management expects Konarc’s margins to further improve by around 6-7 percentage points against Rizta going forward. 

“We could reduce the average ex-showroom price customers experience without affecting gross margins … Konarc is a useful lever that could allow us to improve margins without pushing prices up further, or perhaps reduce the average ex-showroom price a little while maintaining margins, assuming commodities do not ease,” noted Mehta. 

That said, the company is not planning to hike prices barring further cost pressure from commodity inflation. 

The CEO also shed light on how Ather had strategically rolled out Konarc to thread the needle between increasing sales and protecting margins. While the company had initially planned to launch Konarc’s entry-level variants first, the management saw that the demand for their existing 450 and Rizta scooters was outstripping the supply. 

This led to a decision to introduce the mid-level Konarc variants into the market to avoid lower-margin products from cannibalising their demand. Ather now plans to launch Konarc’s entry-level SR1 variant only once their additional capacity in AURIC is online, enabling them to drive volumes without bringing down margins. 

It seems Ather might finally have figured out the key to profitability lies in pricing, cost management, and product mix. Expanding the market through Konarc is another win for the company as well. 

But it still has to overcome the hurdles of commodity costs, effective capacity expansion, and converting demand into deliveries.

item.content:encoded:
Ather’s Profit Milestone Meets A Manufacturing Crunch 

Electric two-wheeler maker Ather Energy turned its maiden profit in Q2 FY27, and now plans to sustain its growth momentum via accelerated investments in its manufacturing capabilities as demand continues to outpace its production. 

Let’s steal a glance at the OEM’s Q2 FY27 numbers:

  • Net profit of ₹1.3 Cr against a net loss of ₹154.1 Cr in Q2 FY26
  • Operating revenue climbed 62.9% to ₹1,464.2 Cr, up 20.3% QoQ
  • EBITDA profit widened to ₹74.2 Cr from ₹9 Cr a year ago
  • Sales of scooters rose 42% YoY to 93,211 units

Other Income Drives Maiden Profit: After 13 years of innovating EV technology, Ather Energy posted its first-ever profitable quarter after turning EBITDA profitable in the preceding quarter as revenue growth far outpaced expenses, which rose 39.4% YoY to ₹1,526 Cr.  However, its operating revenue was ₹61.5 Cr lower than total expenses during the quarter, and the difference was plugged by other income, highlighting a continued quest to improve profitability margins. 

Manufacturing Boost On The Cards: The OEM will invest ₹122 Cr to add 2.25 Lakh units annually to its manufacturing capacity. Its under-construction Factory 3.0 in Maharashtra will receive ₹64 Cr to add 1.5 Lakh units of annual capacity over the planned 5 Lakh units. At its Hosur plant, Ather will invest ₹53 Cr to add capacity for 75,000 units and also set up a new battery line to offset supply chain worries. 

Ather Bleeds On Demand Front: The EV maker believes that it is losing 18,000-20,000 units in demand monthly due to its supply shortfall, with the Hosur plant now operating at 98% capacity and Factory 3.0 yet to go live. This comes as customer enquiries surged 109% YoY to around 10 Lakh, and pre-orders more than doubled to 1.8 Lakh. 

With demand outpacing production and factories nearing capacity, its next challenge is to keep the growth engine running. While we will keep an eye out for just that, here’s how Ather Energy fared in the second quarter of FY27.

From The Editor’s Desk

 Paytm’s Profit Spree

  • The fintech major’s Q2 FY27 net profit surged 10.7X YoY to ₹225 Cr from ₹21 Cr a year ago, edging up from ₹220 Cr in Q1 FY27.
  • Operating revenue grew 28% YoY and 8% QoQ to ₹2,648 Cr, while total expenses rose 23% YoY to ₹2,531 Cr.
  • Paytm’s profitability gains follow a strong Q1 FY27, when net profit rose 78.8% YoY to ₹220 Cr and EBITDA profit jumped 182% to ₹203 Cr, with an EBITDA margin of 8%.

 Imarticus To File ₹1,000 Cr IPO Soon

  • The edtech startup is planning to file its DRHP with SEBI through the confidential route in the next two to three months for a ₹1,000 Cr IPO, up from its earlier ₹750 Cr plan.
  • The company plans to use the proceeds to expand its business, set up more Centres of Excellence, strengthen its School of Finance and Business and B2B operations, and pursue acquisitions. This follows its recent ₹800 Cr acquisition of Singapore’s BELLS Institute of Higher Learning.
  • The IPO plans come amid a slowdown in edtech funding and growing consolidation, with upGrad recently acquiring Unacademy in a deal valuing the startup at just over $200 Mn, down more than 90% from its peak valuation of $3.5 Bn.

 Unacademy Cofounders’ ₹700 Cr VC Play 

  • Gaurav Munjal and Roman Saini are raising ₹700 Cr for Longshot Capital, an early stage fund that has secured ₹250-300 Cr in commitments and is targeting its first close in January 2027.
  • The Bengaluru-based fund plans to back 25-28 AI and deeptech startups at the seed and pre-Series A stages, with initial cheques of 500K-1.5 Mn across sectors such as manufacturing, space, defence and robotics.
  • The move follows upGrad’s acquisition of Unacademy in an all-stock deal valuing the edtech startup at ₹1,955 Cr, over 90% below its peak valuation. The fund also builds on the founders’ track record of over 200 angel investments worth more than ₹25 Cr.

Pronto Founder Finds Her New Gig In AI

  • Anjali Sardana has launched an AI venture, Provision Labs, to collect real-world data for training and testing AI systems designed to perform physical tasks using robots and machines.
  • The launch follows scrutiny over Pronto’s pilot that involved recording household chores to generate robotics training data, raising concerns around customer consent, data privacy and the use of footage.
  • Provision Labs enters a growing market for real-world AI training data, with startups such as Human Archive, Awign and Objectways building pipelines to supply footage of human activities to AI and robotics developers.

Aequs Bloats Its Losses In Q2

  • The contract manufacturer reported a consolidated net loss of ₹52.4 Cr in Q2 FY27, widening 154.4% YoY from ₹20.6 Cr. It reported a net loss of ₹53.2 Cr in Q1.
  • Operating revenue grew 45.3% YoY to ₹409.1 Cr, led by its aerospace business, which contributed ₹351.4 Cr, while consumer business revenue rose 52% to ₹57.7 Cr.
  • Expenses excluding finance costs, depreciation and amortisation surged 56.2% to ₹395.2 Cr, outpacing revenue growth. Sequentially, the net loss narrowed marginally from ₹53.2 Cr in Q1 FY27.

AI Trading Platform Tradl Raises $4.1 Mn 

  • Bengaluru-based Tradl raised $4.1 Mn in a seed round led by Nexus Venture Partners and Stellaris Venture Partners, with participation from angel investors.
  • Founded in 2025 by IIT Guwahati graduates Shubham Bansal and Nilesh Raj, Tradl combines AI and quantitative analysis to help retail traders screen stocks, analyse markets, and backtest strategies.
  • The fundraise comes amid rising investor interest in AI startups, with the segment attracting $438 Mn across 35 deals in Q3 2026, up 265% YoY.

Inc42 Markets

Inc42 Startup Spotlight

Inside Pulse’s Bet To Make Medical Equipment In India

India’s hospitals remain dependent on imported medical devices that can be costly, difficult to service and poorly adapted to local needs. Pulse is trying to build a domestic alternative by combining MSME manufacturing with product design under a single medtech brand.

Going Asset-Light: Founded in 2025, Pulse designs, sources and supplies medical devices and consumables. Instead of owning a large manufacturing base, it provides engineering, product standardisation, certifications, regulatory compliance and service infrastructure to small businesses. This enables these SMEs to build medical equipment that can compete with global manufacturers. 

The Essential Approach: Pulse is initially targeting low- and mid-complexity devices across critical care, renal care and cardiac care. The company is also focusing on mid-tier hospitals, particularly facilities with 50-200 beds, where reliable equipment at accessible prices can have a direct impact on healthcare delivery. 

The Quality Layer: The startup currently works with nearly 20 MSME partners across Delhi NCR, Gujarat, Kolkata and Mumbai. It is also establishing an R&D hub at the Andhra Pradesh MedTech Zone in Visakhapatnam. Going forward, the 3one4 Capital-backed startup plans to scale product development and distribution. 

As hospitals seek affordable and dependable alternatives to imported equipment, can Pulse turn India into a medtech manufacturing hub?

item.content:encoded:
AI-native cybersecurity startup Protectt.ai plans to acquire a controlling stake in AIShield, an AI security platform incubated within Bosch Global Software Technologies (BGSW). Bosch will retain a minority stake in AIShield following the transaction.

Backed by Bessemer Venture Partners, Protectt.ai will acquire the stake through a deal comprising primary and secondary components. The companies have not disclosed the transaction value or timeline.

“There will be cash, a secondary component and future investments as required. The current structure is a combination of cash and ESOPs. Future investments will depend on the requirements of the business,” Protectt.ai cofounder Manish Mimani told Inc42.

Founded in 2022 by Shiv Kumar and Amit Phadke, AIShield was incubated within BGSW. It develops security solutions for machine learning models, generative AI applications and AI supply chains, helping enterprises defend against attacks designed to manipulate AI systems and address compliance risks.

The partnership will combine AIShield’s AI security capabilities with Protectt.ai’s mobile security platform, allowing the latter to expand into enterprise AI security.

AIShield will continue to operate as an independent entity under Protectt.ai once the deal is completed, with its own professional management team and a focus on AI security research and product development. It will also be able to raise external funding in the future.

Protectt.ai plans to work with private companies and government organisations through AIShield to build an India-developed AI security platform, Mimani said.

From Mobile Security To Enterprise AI

Founded in 2020 by Manish Mimani and Mohanraj Selvaraj, Protectt.ai provides mobile threat defence solutions that help businesses protect applications against cyber threats and fraud. Its platform also serves as a compliance hub for app owners, helping them adhere to regulations issued by entities such as the RBI, SEBI and NPCI.

The startup also offers a full-stack AI security platform with tools to test AI agents for vulnerabilities, secure connections between AI applications and external tools, and monitor AI agents while they operate.

Protectt.ai’s security technology runs on more than 1 Bn mobile devices and processes 15 Bn mobile application sessions every month, Mimani said.

He expects mobile applications to increasingly rely on AI agents to perform tasks, potentially reducing the need for users to navigate conventional app interfaces over the next one to two years.

Protectt.ai had already been researching AI model scanning and AI agent security as part of its product roadmap. Through the AIShield acquisition, the startup aims to extend these capabilities beyond mobile applications to enterprise use cases across sectors.

Some members of Protectt.ai’s AI security team will move to AIShield, although the number has yet to be finalised.

AIShield currently has around 12–15 employees and plans to expand its team to 50–60 people by March 2027. It plans to hire PhD researchers, master’s graduates and other technical talent from leading institutions to strengthen its research and engineering capabilities.

The team will focus on developing products, conducting research and filing patents, Mimani said.

Protectt.ai Eyes Further Acquisitions

The AIShield deal is Protectt.ai’s first such acquisition. The startup set up an M&A team earlier in 2026 to evaluate potential acquisitions and partnerships, with a focus on building capabilities and addressing gaps in its existing offerings.

Protectt.ai is exploring opportunities in areas such as API security and cloud security that could complement its current capabilities, Mimani said.

The startup secured around $16 Mn in a Series A funding round led by Bessemer Venture Partners and Bajaj Finance in 2025. Mimani added that Protectt.ai is evaluating opportunities and expects to consider raising fresh funds in 2027.

item.dc:creator: Team Inc42
item.description: AI-powered healthtech platform BioStack has raised $9.5 Mn (₹90.4 Cr) in its seed funding round led by Peak XV Partners,…
item.content:encoded:
AI-powered healthtech platform BioStack has raised $9.5 Mn (₹90.4 Cr) in its seed funding round led by Peak XV Partners, Afore Capital, DCVC, Emerson Collective, SV Angel, Verdict Capital, Streamlined Ventures, and Y Combinator. 

The startup plans to utilise the fresh capital to continue expanding its presence in the US and other international markets, including India, Brazil, and Argentina. A chunk of the capital will also be used to scale its tech stack and ramp up hiring across engineering and research teams.

Founded in 2025 by Sanat Mishra and Parth Patwa, BioStack claims to be building the data infrastructure for the next generation of medical AI. 

It combines fragmented clinical information across systems such as electronic health records, medical imaging, clinical notes and medications. The startup then uses this data to create proprietary datasets for research, biotechnology, and the development and training of medical AI models.

“We’re building the infrastructure that connects all of the clinical information and makes it useful, both for clinicians making decisions today and for the researchers and AI developers building the future of medicine,” said BioStack cofounder and CEO Mishra.

BioStack currently works with multiple hospitals across the US, Brazil and Argentina. In India, it is also connecting cancer patients with an investigational cancer vaccine program. 

The startup also claims that it offers use cases such as AI model evaluation, disease modeling, biomarker discovery, patient stratification and treatment-response analysis.

Besides offering custom workflows to protect patient privacy, the startup claims to have so far processed 10 Cr de-identified patient records, more than “several hundred thousand” fragmented X-Rays, MRIs and CT scans, and “several million” telehealth audio transcripts. 

For context, de-identified patient records are medical datasets that have had all personal and direct identifiers removed so that the individual cannot reasonably be linked to the data.

The fundraise comes as India becomes a training ground to collect datasets for powering AI models and physical AI products. Startups are tapping India’s huge population to collect recordings of workers performing physical tasks, processing the footage, and selling the resulting datasets to frontier AI labs and robotics companies.

For instance, the likes of Awign, Objectways and Human Archive are building pipelines to supply first-person footage of human activity to AI developers. Just a day ago, instant home services startup Pronto’s founder Anjali Sardana launched Provision Labs, a US-based venture to collect data for physical AI systems.

At the heart of all this is the Indian AI training dataset, which is projected to become a $1.3 Bn opportunity by 2033.

item.content:encoded:
Social gaming platform Matiks has raised $10 Mn (₹95.1 Cr) in its Pre-Series A funding round led by General Catalyst. 

The round also saw participation from upGrad founder Ronnie Screwvala as well as existing backers such as Info Edge Ventures, Tanglin Venture Partners and Untitled Ventures.

In a statement, the startup said that it plans to utilise the fresh capital to expand its global footprint and invest in new games and social experiences. The fresh funding will also be used to deepen investments in engineering, AI, product, design and growth. 

A chunk of the capital will also be utilised to build an AI-powered engine, which will enable users to build and publish their own social games without writing code. Going forward, it has also set its eyes on scaling creator partnerships, global distribution and player community.

“… We started Matiks with a simple belief: using your brain can be just as fun and addictive as any other form of entertainment. Our ambition is to make mind sports as culturally relevant as physical sports and esports – giving mental athletes, puzzlers, and competitive players the visibility, communities, and recognition they deserve…,” said Matiks cofounder and CEO Sudhanshu Bhatia.

Founded in 2024 by Bhatia, Mohan Kumar and Sushant Timmapur, Matiks is an esports platform that allows users to play social games spanning mathematics, memory, logic and puzzles. It also allows users to compete with each other. 

The startup claims that more than 22 Lakh players had played 4.8 Cr games on its platform as of September 2026. Matiks also claimed that its daily active users currently hover around 3 Lakh, with early engagement also emerging from international markets such as Japan, the US and South Korea.

The startup last raised $3.14 Mn in its pre-Series A round led by Tanglin Ventures in August last year.

Going forward, the startup plans to initially prioritise expansion in the US before entering more tier I markets. Its future roadmap also includes building its AI-powered game creation engine, which the startup believes will foster adoption and create new experiences.

The fundraise comes as India’s gaming market is expanding beyond the usual battle royale and casual games. Buoyed by 51 Cr gamers, the ban on real-money games last year, the rise of AI and regulatory push for social games, the homegrown gaming arena is seeing renewed traction and interest from investors.

Earlier this month, mobile gaming studio Spill Games raised $10.5 Mn in its Series A round led by Elevation Capital. In April this year, another gaming studio LightFury Games also bagged $11 Mn in its pre-Series A funding round from Blume Ventures and others.

In August, cricketer Rohit Sharma also joined LightFury Games as an investor, alongside MS Dhoni, Jasprit Bumrah, and Hardik Pandya, among others. 

At the heart of all this is the Indian gaming market, which is projected to become a $9.9 Bn opportunity by 2031.
